standard.title: Physical Changes to Materials
standard.description: recognise that materials can be changed physically without changing their material composition and explore the effect of different actions on materials including bending, twisting, stretching and breaking into smaller pieces
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can observe and describe properties of materials (AC9SFU03, F band). They have not yet distinguished between changing the form of a material and changing its composition, or systematically explored multiple physical change actions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise that physical actions (bending, twisting, stretching, folding, cutting, crushing) change the shape or size of a material without changing what it is made of, and explore how different materials respond differently to the same physical action.

nodes.label: Physical changes alter shape without changing composition
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that physically changing a material (bending, twisting, stretching, breaking) changes its shape or size but not what it is made of.
nodes.minimum_width: Students demonstrate at least two physical changes to a material and explain that the material is still the same substance after the change.
nodes.typical_width: Students manipulate materials (paper, fabric, playdough, wool); apply multiple physical changes (scrunching, twisting, bending, cutting, tearing, folding); explain that the material is still the same even though its shape has changed; and compare the properties of the original and changed material.
wider: Crush a stick of chalk into powder — comparing properties of the stick and powder and discussing whether it is still the same material
Explore how First Nations Australians make physical changes to natural materials to produce objects such as bowls, baskets and fibre crafts — examining purposeful physical transformation
Create an 'odd one out' game using samples of the same material changed in different ways plus one different material — applying composition knowledge to a classification challenge
nodes.hinge_reason: N2 requires students to accept that physical action changes form but not composition before they can reason about why different materials respond differently to the same action. Without the composition-vs-form distinction, students conflate different physical outcomes with different materials — blocking the comparison at N2.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly believe that dramatically changing the shape of a material (crushing chalk, folding paper into a plane) creates a different material. Making the composition-vs-form distinction explicit — the shape changes, what it is made of does not — is the essential conceptual scaffold before students can correctly distinguish physical from chemical change in later years.

success_criteria: Applies at least two physical changes to a material and names each action
Explains that the material is still the same substance after a physical change — only its shape or size has changed

nodes.label: Different actions affect materials differently
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore and describe how different physical actions affect different materials and explain how physical changes can be purposeful.
nodes.minimum_width: Students compare how the same action affects two different materials and describe the result of each.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate how different materials respond to the same actions (twisting cotton wool vs paper vs fabric); explore how physical changes can be purposeful (twisting strands of cotton to make thread stronger, folding paper to make it fly); and describe multiple ways the same material can be physically changed.
wider: Explore how materials can be physically changed to suit a particular purpose — twisting cotton to make thread stronger, folding paper to make it fly
Learn from people who work with materials (woodworkers, fibre artists, sculptors) about how they learn about material properties and use creativity when manipulating them (AC9S2H01)
Explore how physically changing materials helps us re-use them — connecting physical change to waste reduction

response_modes.reason: Material worker perspectives (AC9S2H01) and purposeful change directions provide authentic real-world connections that show physical transformation as intentional and contextually meaningful — enriching the concept beyond classroom manipulation tasks.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Material worker perspectives (AC9S2H01) provide an authentic real-world direction. The purposeful change direction connects physical transformation to design intent.
success_criteria: Compares how the same physical action affects two different materials
Describes at least one physical change that is purposeful — explaining why the change is useful
